chunks: What a LiPo C rating means. The question: What is a LiPo's C rating?
The C rating says how much current a battery can deliver, as a multiple of its capacity. 1C is the current that would empty the battery in exactly one hour.
A 10C battery can deliver ten times that current. It is a way of comparing batteries of different sizes, and it tells you how hard you can push one.
Think of a water tank and a tap. If the tank holds 100 liters and the tap runs 100 liters per hour, the tank empties in one hour. That is 1C.
Open the tap to ten times that rate and the tank is empty in six minutes, which is 10C. A bigger flow needs a stronger pipe.
For a battery, the "pipe" is its internal resistance, and pushing too much current through it makes heat, not just a faster drain.
Heat grows with the square of the C-rate: going from 10C to 30C multiplies the current by 3 and the heat by 9. This quadratic climb is why "burst" ratings must be time-limited.
Efficiency at 30C is about 82 % in this example, i. e. , about 18 % of the energy becomes heat.
Drag the resistance up to 20 milliohms: heat at every C-rate doubles and the 30C efficiency drops below 65%.
Capacity: how much charge the battery holds, in amp-hours (Ah) or milliamp-hours (mAh) ("How battery capacity is measured"). Current: how much charge flows per second, in amps.
C-rate: current divided by capacity (in Ah). 2 amps from a 2 Ah cell is 1C. Continuous vs burst rating: the current you can draw all the time versus for a few seconds.
Internal resistance: the cell's own opposition to current, which limits current and makes heat ("Battery internal resistance").
Take a 2200 milliamp hours pack, which is 2. 2 Ah. 1C is 2. 2 amps, and it lasts about 60 minutes. A 10C draw is 10 times 2. 2 equals 22 amps, which would last about 6 minutes.
A 30C rating means up to 30 times 2. 2 equals 66 amps, for about 2 minutes. If the cell has 10 milliohms of resistance, 66 amps makes about 66 squared times 0.
01 equals 44 watts of heat inside it. That is the whole idea.
"The C rating is the maximum current as a multiple of the battery's capacity.
1C is the current that would empty it in an hour, so a 2200 milliamp-hour 30C pack can deliver 30 times 2. 2, or 66 amps, and runs flat in two minutes.
It's really a limit set by internal resistance and heat: at 66 amps the cell sags and dissipates tens of watts.
Ratings usually come as continuous and burst, they aren't standardized, so I size by dividing peak current by capacity, add margin, and verify sag and temperature."
